zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check: NINJAL, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, supplied package subset; CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Dataset: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html. The scan, not the lexical index or generated kana hints, determines the diplomatic text.

lines.note: Ganyei denotes a haze or film over the eyes; the Portuguese reads Neuoa, not a modernized névoa. This is the entry anticipated by the preceding page's separate Gan- catchword.
Cauobaxe and catachi give facial appearance and form, matching the Portuguese rosto. The circumflex in Ganyô and the two Japanese synonyms are retained; the gloss continues below.
Figura completes the preceding definition of facial appearance. S. is an upright usage label, not part of the italic gloss; the irregular ink to its right does not form another textual line.

Ganzǒ is the mixture entry, with fucumi majiuaru expressing inclusion and intermixture. The damaged letter after maji is read as u rather than OCR n: its remaining stems, the verb majiwaru, and the mixed-fish gloss agree. The initial is G, and igua continues as ria without an added hyphen.

runs.text: ria de muitos pexes miſturados feitos em Saxi-

lines.note: Ria completes iguaria: a dish of several kinds of fish mixed and prepared as sashimi. The scan supports miſturados rather than miſturidos. The embedded Japanese Saxi- is actually italic here and breaks at the printed hyphen.

Italic mi completes Saxi-mi, followed by the upright S. label. The next sense begins with Miſtura, whose narrow i is visible rather than OCR e, and extends the meaning to a mixture of different things.
Couſas completes the general mixture sense of Ganzǒ. This short continuation is a full physical body row, distinct from the next headword.
Gappato is labelled an adverb and referred to Gafato, the preceding entry for an unexpected or sudden occurrence. The cross-reference remains roman, while Adu. Vide is italic.
The headword is Gappi, not OCR Ganpi: both p descenders can be seen and the example repeats the same form. Gappi ſuru means to agree or correspond, as the Portuguese explains across the next line.
The example Gappi ſuru is translated as fitting or having correspondence. The historical correſpondencia spelling is preserved, with no new entry implied by this indented continuation.

runs.text: Almas famintas que eſtão no Inferno ſe

lines.note: Gaqi is gaki, the hungry spirits described in the Portuguese, not OCR Guqi. The final ſe is the beginning of ſegundo on the next row; no terminal hyphen is supplied where none is printed.

runs.text: gundo a opinião dos gentios. ¶ Item, Per

lines.note: Gundo completes ſegundo and attributes this description to the beliefs of the people the dictionary calls gentios. Per begins the metaphorical-usage label completed by met. below; both fragments remain on their physical rows.

The figurative sense is a hungry, thin, wasted person. Reinspection distinguishes eſfaimada from OCR eſtaimada and the first long ſ in deſfeita from f; both readings agree with the linked description of hunger.
The description adds a pale or discoloured appearance, then begins another usage of the word as an insult. The historical deſcorada and He are retained rather than modernized.
This continues the explanation that Gaqi can rebuke and belittle someone, and introduces a Japanese example. The ampersand and final Vt, remain in the italic Portuguese apparatus.
Ano gaqimega is the contemptuous expression illustrated by the Portuguese description of a wretched person. The supplied st treatment in triste is retained, and the printed mala- continues below.
Venturado completes malaventurado, followed by the alternative meaning faminto, hungry. The printed line break and concluding &c. are preserved.

This separate Gaqi entry gives hunger, with Vye and vyuru corresponding to hunger and being hungry. The gloss Fome is italic but its S. label is upright; it is not merged with the preceding spirits entry.

runs.text: Inferno onde a tormentão com fome

lines.note: Gaqidǒ is the hungry-ghost realm, explained as a hell in which souls are tormented with hunger. The scan's a tormentão spacing is retained as printed rather than silently joining the Portuguese verb.
As almas supplies the object of tormentão in the preceding line. This brief continuation completes Gaqidǒ before the unrelated suffix Gara begins.

runs.text: Modo, feição: ſempre vai com outro

lines.note: Gara expresses a manner or character and is explained as occurring with another noun. The colon and long ſ in ſempre are retained; the construction continues below.
Tocorogara illustrates a place's character. The last letters are fei, not OCR fer, beginning feição across the following physical row without an invented hyphen.

runs.text: ção do lugar. No Cami ſe diz.

lines.note: Ção completes feição do lugar. The explanation says that in Cami the form is Tocorocara; Cami is embedded in the Portuguese and is visibly italic here, whereas the cited alternative is roman. The spurious split italic span inside diz is removed.
Iibungara gives a time or conjunction of circumstances. The initial Ii spelling is preserved, and the Portuguese tẽ is the nasal abbreviation continuing with po on the next line.

runs.text: po em que ha algum trabalho, ou particulari-

lines.note: Po completes tẽpo. The definition specifies a time involving some difficulty or particular circumstance; particulari- retains its visible dividing hyphen.
Dade completes particularidade and closes the Iibungara explanation. The short continuation and its &c. are retained as their own body row.

Garagarato is the rattling or clattering adverb. The explanation introduces the sound of bells and related objects; the faint internal letters remain consistent with Garagarato, and cam- continues below.
Painhas completes campainhas, followed by rattles, small objects and nuts as sources of the sound. The original caſcaueis and trebelhos are retained rather than replaced by modern vocabulary.

Garamecaxi is the causative entry for making these things rattle. The scan has initial G, not C, but visibly prints u in the conjugational sequence; that anomalous ending is retained instead of supplying the grammatically expected ſu. Cou- continues on the next row.

runs.text: ſas, ou cauſar qualquer outra traquinada.

lines.note: The definition adds causing any other disturbance or clatter. Qualquer is one printed word, not OCR qual juer; the historical traquinada is retained, and ſas completes couſas from above.
Garameqi is the corresponding intransitive verb for sounding or making a disturbance. Its u, eita sequence is retained; fazerẽ keeps its nasal mark and tra- continues below.
Quinada completes traquinada, with rats as the first example. A further sense concerns bells and similar objects; the ending cam has no added hyphen because the scan does not clearly print one.
Painhas completes the repeated reference to campainhas. The sequence of trebelhos, caſcaueis and nozes supplies further rattling objects, closing the intransitive Garameqi entry.
Garan denotes a large temple or temple establishment. The short Portuguese definition and the headword's initial G are clearly separate from the surrounding sound-symbolic entries.

runs.text: Adu. Modo de ſoar algũa couſa

lines.note: Gararito is another adverb describing how an object sounds. The mark in algũa is retained, and its illustrative comparison with bells continues below.
This completes Gararito with the sound of a bell or rattles. The supplied historical spelling caſcaueis and the final &c. remain unchanged.
The reduplicated Gararigararito is labelled an adverb with the same meaning as Gararito. The repeated sequence is preserved in full rather than collapsed into the shorter headword.

runs.text: Vuas do mato q̃ cõmũmente chama-

lines.note: Garenbu names wild grapes. Enlarging the damaged letter before b shows the surviving upper/right stroke of n rather than a joined lower bowl of u; the supplied NINJAL index also identifies Garenbu. Vuas, q̃ and cõmũmente retain their historical spelling and abbreviations, with chama- continuing below.

Mos completes chamamos; the explanation gives garebo, an alternative Gara, and the Cami name Yabu-budo. The different printed fonts are retained: garebo and alicubi are italic, Gara and Cami are roman, and Yabu- ends at the visible hyphen.
Budo completes Yabu-budo, the regional name embedded in the preceding Portuguese explanation. The roman continuation is kept on its own printed row, without supplying an unprinted vowel-length mark.

runs.text: Adu. Modo de ſoar couſa du-

lines.note: Garigarito describes a hard crunching sound. The Portuguese explicitly begins to qualify the sounding object as dura, with du- retaining its printed division.
Ra completes dura, and the gloss specifies something that crunches between the teeth. The q̃ abbreviation remains as printed rather than expanded to que.

Gariǒji describes forcibly taking something while asserting ownership, as the continuation explains. The scan supports the headword and zuru despite local weak inking; the long-o mark is retained as supplied.

runs.text: & repunando outros inſiſtindo que he ſua, ou

lines.note: The definition adds opposition from others and insistence that the thing is one's own. The scan supports inſiſtindo rather than OCR inſiſindo; repunando and he retain their historical printed forms.
This completes the possessive claim made by the person taking the object. The plural lhes is preserved as printed, not adjusted to a modern paraphrase of the entry.

Gariqi means one's own strength. The explanatory Japanese would be understood as waga chikara, but this copy visibly reads Vaga hi ara with the consonants not legible; the defective printed sequence is retained rather than silently reconstructed.

The example means doing it by one's own strength. Initial G and the visible caron in tçucamaçurǒ replace OCR C and circumflex; Farei cõ is visibly separated, and mi continues as nhas at the top of column 2 without an invented hyphen.
Nhas completes minhas from the bottom of column 1, closing the translation of Gariqide tçucamaçurǒ. The X. label is wholly upright rather than leaving its period in a stray italic span.
Gatamecaxi is the causative verb for making something rattle. Unlike the anomalous u printed in Garamecaxi, this row visibly supplies ſu, aita; the Portuguese alternatives continue below.

runs.text: ſoar couſas duras, ou ſecas. ¶ Item, Fa-

lines.note: The objects made to sound are hard or dry things. A further sense begins with Fa-, whose printed hyphen divides Fazer at the next physical row.
Zer completes Fazer, adding the making of doors and similar things sound. The historical long ſ in ſoar and final &c. are retained.
Gatameqi gives the corresponding intransitive clattering or rattling. The u, eita conjugational sequence is distinct from the causative entry above, and the definition carries into the next row.
The Portuguese refers back to the same sounding objects, then introduces Votogaiga gatamequ, the jaw or chin chattering. The Japanese verb is physically divided after ga- at the visible hyphen.

runs.text: Soarem os queixos quando hũ tre-

lines.note: Tamequ completes gatamequ. The translation explains jaws chattering when someone trembles, with hũ retaining its nasal abbreviation and tre- continuing on the next row.

Me completes treme, specifying cold as the cause. Gatagatato ſuru supplies an equivalent sound-symbolic expression; the small terminal mark has a visible descending tail and is transcribed as the printed comma.
Lowercase idem assigns Gatagatato ſuru the same meaning as the jaw-chattering example. The brief gloss occupies its own body row and is not part of the next headword.

Gatera is illustrated by Qenbutgaterani, going to look at something while taking the opportunity to do so. The Japanese historical Qenbut spelling is retained; oca- begins the Portuguese ocasião across the line break.

runs.text: ſião de ir ver: não ſe vſa eſta palaura por ſi ſe

lines.note: The opening ſião completes ocasião: the scan shows the dotted i and the tilde over a, not OCR ſũão. The explanation says Gatera is not used by itself, and the final ſe continues as ſenão below.
Não completes ſenão, specifying use together with other words. No hyphen or new sentence is inserted into the printed cross-line construction.
Gattai denotes joining or uniting, with Taiuo auaſuru expressing bringing bodies together. The historical spellings auaſuru and vnir are preserved.
The example describes sharing a united intention or mind. Dôxinno carries the visible circumflex, vomoiuo retains its historical onset, and Eſ- begins the Portuguese Eſtar below.

runs.text: tar vnido no coração, & vontade com outro.

lines.note: Tar completes Eſtar, translating the example as being united with another in heart and will. The original vnido and conjunction punctuation are retained.
The headword is Gatten, with a visible G rather than OCR C. It denotes understanding, and Gatten itaita is the first example, followed by a printed comma connecting it to the next expression.
The second example is translated as having understood. The scan really prints gaetenni, with e after ga, rather than the expected gattenni; this apparent printing anomaly is deliberately retained.
A further sense is approval or assent, with the alternative tenuo auaſuru. The isolated italic A starts Aprouar on the next row; no missing hyphen is invented.

runs.text: prouar, ou conſentir em algũa couſa aßinando,

lines.note: Prouar completes Aprouar, defining consent with a signature as one possibility. Algũa and aßinando retain their printed nasal and doubled-s forms.
This adds that consent may also be given without signing. The two separate ſe forms and aßinar close the approval sense, not a new entry.

Gauô groups Ga and voxidori, birds glossed here as a duck and another colourful bird. The circumflex and voxidori spelling are preserved; paſſa- continues below rather than being expanded within this row.
Ro completes paſſaro and describes the second bird as having various colours. The row completes the bird entry before Gaxi begins.
Gaxi is death by starvation, explained by the Japanese Vye, xiſuru and Portuguese Morrer de fome. The comma in the Japanese paraphrase is retained rather than recast as modern prose.
Gaxini voyobu describes reaching the point of death from hunger. The Portuguese phrase remains incomplete until fome on the following physical row.
Fome completes the translation of Gaxini voyobu. This single-word continuation is retained as body text with its own crop, not mistaken for furniture or a separate headword.
Gaxxi means combining or joining, with ſuru and xita giving the verb's forms. The first example concerns combining ingredients or materials, as specified below; the paired x letters are retained.

The materials are those used for mezinhas, remedies, followed by a figurative sense. The print's Itẽ abbreviation and joined Permet. are retained; V- is the beginning of Vnirſe, not a standalone label.
Nirſe completes Vnirſe, giving the figurative meaning of uniting in friendship. The historical initial V stays in the previous physical row.
The headword is Gaxxǒ, not OCR Cuxxǒ: the G and a are visible, and Tanagocorouo auaſuru describes bringing the palms together. The definition of joining the hands continues below.
The gesture is joining the hands in worship. Chǒqi gaxxǒ xite introduces kneeling with the palms joined; the supplied long-o marks and the printed xi- division are retained.

runs.text: Pondoſe de joelhos, & com as mãos ale

lines.note: Te completes xite, followed by the translation of kneeling and holding the hands raised. Ale begins aleuantadas across the next row without an added hyphen.
Uantadas completes the historical form aleuantadas. This continuation closes the worship-gesture example before the separate architectural Gaxxǒ entry.

runs.text: Hũs paos altos da caſa co-

lines.note: This homonymous Gaxxǒ is glossed by Saſu and refers to high structural timbers of a house. The i, synonym label is retained, and co- begins the comparison completed below.
Mo completes como aſnas, comparing the timbers to roof trusses or their members. The long ſ in aſnas is preserved; it is not the adjective altas or a new Japanese word.
Gaxxǒqin denotes foods said not to combine well. The definition continues across the next line; this is the dictionary's historical dietary description, not a modern recommendation.

runs.text: ſi, ou que fazem mal aquem os come juntos.

lines.note: The foods are said to disagree with one another or harm someone eating them together. The printed aquem remains joined, and the gloss is kept as a report of the source's wording.

The clearly printed pilcrow, omitted by OCR, introduces a metaphorical application to people. Cano fitoto, ano fitoua begins a sentence about incompatible natures, and gax- continues the compound on the next row.
Xǒqinde aru completes gaxxǒqinde aru. The translation states that those people do not agree in their natures, whose final noun follows below; the roman example and italic gloss remain distinct.
Naturezas closes the first metaphorical example. The new sentence Areua vaga gaxxǒqin introduces someone incompatible with the speaker; its copula follows on the next row.
Gia completes the Japanese sentence. The Portuguese metaphor contra peçonha is retained literally as printed; the context is personal incompatibility, not instructions involving poison.
Gayocu is explained by Gano tçubaſa and the Portuguese wings of a duck. The final S. is upright, outside the italic definition, and the original ç and long ſ are retained.

This Gue means low or inferior, with Xita and cudaru as the Japanese explanation. It begins the Gue sequence without an extra section heading or enlarged initial; the printed running header above still reads G ANTES DO A.

runs.text: Sentença, ou verſo como o que diße cada

lines.note: The separate Gue means a sentence or verse. The Portuguese starts an analogy involving what each apostle said; the historical diße remains unchanged.

The word is Apoſtolo, not OCR Aposholo, with a tall joined st cluster provisionally rendered ſt. The faint right curve after çã supports final o in cõpoſição; the analogy concerns the composition of the creed. Ichi begins a roman Japanese example continued below.
Gue completes Ichi gue, one sentence or one verse. The source alternates Hũa and hum here; both are retained, and the weak nasal mark in Hũa is not regularized away.
Gueba is dismounting, explained by Vma yori voruru. The historical voruru and Decerſe remain as printed, and caua- carries the Portuguese word for horse to the next row.

runs.text: lo diãte de peßoa de reſpeito, ou dalgũa

lines.note: Lo completes caualo: the rider dismounts before a respected person or a Tera as courtesy. The embedded Japanese Tera is visibly roman within the italic Portuguese; diãte and dalgũa preserve their nasal marks.
Corteſia completes the reason for dismounting. The separate signature F f 3 and far-right Gue- catchword are page furniture on the same horizontal band, not continuations of this body line.
